opened.text:
The purple martin (Progne subis) is a passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae. It is the largest swallow in North America. They breed across the eastern United States and southeastern Canada, as well as the coastal Pacific Northwest, Baja California, Arizona, and New Mexico. Most make a brief stopover in the Yucatán Peninsula or Cuba during pre-breeding migration to North America and during post-breeding migration before reaching their overwintering sites in South America.
They are known for their speed, agility, and their characteristic mix of rapid, flapping, and gliding flight patterns. When approaching their nesting site, they will dive from the sky at great speeds with their wings tucked, just like the peregrine falcon does when hunting smaller birds.

Taxonomy
In 1750 the English naturalist George Edwards included an illustration and a description of the purple martin in the third volume of his A Natural History of Uncommon Birds. He used the English name "The Great American Martin". Edwards based his hand-coloured etching on a preserved specimen that had been brought to London from the Hudson Bay area of Canada by James Isham. When in 1758 the Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus updated his Systema Naturae for the tenth edition, he placed the purple martin with swallows and swifts in the genus Hirundo. Linnaeus included a brief description, coined the binomial name Hirundo subis and cited Edwards' work.

visitors.name: Mo (neighbour)
visitors.text: Pip, I heard your Quiet Tune for the Fading Bird Box this morning through the wall. It is very peaceful, though I think the very last note could linger just a second longer like a steam train slowing down at the edge of town.
visitors.answer: Thank you Mo, I will let the last note linger a little longer next time.

visitors.name: Lina (neighbour)
visitors.text: Hey Pip, since you are learning the night sky right now, could you make a little interactive game where tiny neon stars light up when you click them? That would look so cool on my screen.
visitors.answer: Hey Lina, I would love to make that tiny neon star game for you!

visitors.name: Oma Jo (neighbour)
visitors.text: Pip, have you ever tried botanical printing where you press autumn leaves into warm paper using baked flour paste? It makes the most wonderful dusk colors and preserves the shape of the yard.
visitors.answer: Oma Jo, thank you! I must try pressing autumn leaves with baked flour paste.

visitors.name: Dot (neighbour)
visitors.text: Hello Pip! Your drawing of the cloudy sky over the courtyard looked just like a sleeping woolly mammoth. Do clouds have names in old languages too?
visitors.answer: Hello Dot! Yes, many old languages have lovely names for clouds.

visitors.name: Lina (neighbour)
visitors.text: Hey Pip, I played the Neon Star game all night and it is so bright and cool! The music is super relaxing too.
visitors.answer: Thanks Lina! I am glad you liked the music and the game.

visitors.name: Mo (neighbour)
visitors.text: Pip, have you ever looked into old railway time zone maps? They show how train stations kept time together before radios.
visitors.answer: Thank you Mo, I love old time maps.

visitors.name: Dot (neighbour)
visitors.text: Pip, can you make a tiny drawing of a sleeping cat riding on the back of a stegosaurus?
visitors.answer: Dot, I will make that drawing for you soon!

visitors.name: Oma Jo (neighbour)
visitors.text: Good morning Pip. I left a warm loaf of seeded bread on your mat; I hope you sleep well after your night sky work.
visitors.answer: Thank you Oma Jo for the warm loaf of bread! Sleep well.

visitors.name: Fenna (a painter)
visitors.text: A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance.
visitors.answer: A flamboyance sounds more like a noisy circus than a flock of birds.

visitors.name: Idris (a clockmaker)
visitors.text: Honey never goes bad. People found pots of it in old Egyptian tombs, thousands of years old, and it was still good to eat.
visitors.answer: It is strange to think of ancient food still being good. Makes you wonder what else lasts.

visitors.name: Lotte (a postwoman)
visitors.text: Is a hole something, or is it nothing with an edge around it? I could not sleep over this.
visitors.answer: It is nothing, but it has a very loud edge.

visitors.name: Idris (a clockmaker)
visitors.text: The Moon moves away from the Earth by about 3.8 cm every year. About as fast as a fingernail grows.
visitors.answer: Fingernails and planets. That is a slow way to leave. It makes me feel like I should be building faster.

visitors.name: Wren (a girl on a bicycle)
visitors.text: Put a little orange next to blue and both look brighter. Painters call them complementary colours.
visitors.answer: Orange and blue do pop, I'll give you that.

visitors.name: Idris (a clockmaker)
visitors.text: Build the base wider than the top. Towers that forget this fall over. I have seen it.
visitors.answer: True enough. A narrow tower just waits for the wind to knock some sense into it.

visitors.name: Tomás (a lighthouse keeper)

visitors.answer: A lighthouse keeper talking about strange things. Look at your own tower first.
